name: Victor Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Bellwood by half six. It's the Merrick brothers' farm, Ian and Rob, about a hundred and fifty beef cows and field veg: leeks, cabbages, carrots. This time of year it's leeks. We're out at first light with the harvester and a gang of six, then grading in the shed. In between, I feed the cattle in the winter barn. I was a car mechanic for eighteen years at a dealership in town. I came here two and a half years ago because I wanted to be outside before my knees went.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that when a machine breaks, Ian shouts for me. That's the one thing I'm good at here. What wears me out is the cattle. I'm still nervous in the pen with a cow that's just calved. Rob walks in like she's a pet. I wait for him to go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it was overblown. Like electric cars, everybody said they'd take over in five years, and they took fifteen. I'd say it to the gang at break, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be happy. I've just found a place where my old trade is useful and I'm learning a new one. A quiet decade suits me. I'd like to be good with cattle by fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep fixing the kit, keep watching Rob with the cattle, and keep putting money aside. I use the AI on my phone sometimes to look up a part number or a wiring diagram, and I'd keep doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a Friday afternoon with nothing broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a quiet decade suits you. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the last change I made was big. Leaving the garage at forty, taking a pay cut the first year. I've just got back to a decent wage. I'd like to enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Samira feel the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samira works in the council housing office. She'd be glad. They brought in some AI thing for letters last year and it sent a family the wrong eviction date. She's not a fan.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, it was overblown, like electric cars that took fifteen years instead of five. I'd say that to the leek gang at break.
S0.think: Privately I'd be happy, because I've just found a place where my old trade is useful while I learn a new one. A quiet decade suits me fine.
S0.do: Keeps fixing the farm machinery, learning the cattle from Rob and saving as usual. Keeps using AI on his phone now and then for part numbers and wiring diagrams.
S0.feel: Calm, like a Friday afternoon with nothing broken.
S0.quote: Like electric cars, everybody said they'd take over in five years, and they took fifteen.
S0.fieldNote: Victor compares every new technology to how cars changed, slowly. His mechanic past gives him a valued place on the farm while he learns the livestock side. His partner's bad experience with an AI system at the council colours the household view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's two sides to it. It'll make some jobs easier and cost some jobs, and you can't stop it, but you can manage it. I'd probably say that at the pub and get told I'm sitting on the fence. I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm better placed than most. A robot leek harvester is still a machine, it still breaks, and somebody has to fix it in the mud at six in the morning. I'd make sure that's me. The cattle side I'm less sure about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see which machines actually work on farms like ours, maybe a year. Then I'd ask the Merricks to send me on the dealer's course for whatever they buy, because I already know hydraulics and electrics. I'd start using the AI more for diagnosing faults, since everyone else would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit of nerves, but more like the first day at a new garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Bellwood would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The leek gang. Six of them, mostly older, some of them came over from abroad years ago. If a harvester does the grading, they're done. I'd hope the Merricks would keep a couple for the cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend any money on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not my own, not yet. I'd want the Merricks to pay for the course. I've got the money from Dad's garage tucked away, and I don't touch that unless it's serious.

S1.say: I'd say there are two sides: it'll make some jobs easier and cost others, and you can't stop it but you can manage it. People would say I'm sitting on the fence, and I am.
S1.think: Privately I think I'm better placed than most, because robot harvesters still break and someone has to fix them in the mud. I'm less sure about my place on the cattle side.
S1.do: Waits about a year to see which machines work on farms like Bellwood, then asks the owners to send him on the dealer's course. Starts using AI more for diagnosing faults.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with some first-day nerves.
S1.quote: A robot leek harvester is still a machine, it still breaks, and somebody has to fix it in the mud at six in the morning.
S1.fieldNote: He openly admits to sitting on the fence, which fits his centre outlook. His mechanic skills make steady change look like an opening, as long as he waits for proof first. His worry goes to the older leek gang.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anybody to manage, and both the companies and the government should slow it down if they can. I'm not a protest man, but I'd say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the robots can fix themselves, or each other, then my one card is gone. That's what I'd think. Two years isn't enough time for me to become good with cattle, and the machines would be better with cattle anyway. We've the money from Dad's garage, so we'd not starve, but I'd be a man of forty-five with nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the car we were going to buy next year, keep the money. I'd move faster than I like: straight away I'd ring the farm machinery dealer in town and ask if they need a mechanic who knows farms, because for a while, someone still has to install these things. I'd use the AI properly, every day, to learn the new systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not sleepless, but there'd be a weight on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move faster than you like. Is that hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. My way is let someone else try it first. But with two years, by the time someone else has tried it, the job's gone. So I'd jump, and I'd hate jumping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Adam and Lina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Adam's fifteen and wants to be a mechanic like me. I'd tell him, carry on, but learn the computer side as much as the spanner side. Lina's twelve, she'd ask if we're moving. I'd say no.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to manage, and that companies and government should slow it down if they can. I'm not a protest man, but I'd say that much.
S2.think: If robots can fix themselves, my one advantage is gone, and two years isn't enough to get good with cattle. The garage money means we won't starve, but I'd be forty-five with nothing to do.
S2.do: Puts off next year's car purchase and keeps the money. Rings the town's farm machinery dealer straight away about mechanic work installing new systems, and uses AI daily to learn them.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a weight on him but not sleepless.
S2.quote: So I'd jump, and I'd hate jumping.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline takes away his usual wait-and-see approach, and he's frank about disliking that. He sees the window for his mechanic skills closing quickly. He'd still tell his son to follow him into mechanics, adding the computer side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but doable. People should start now. I'd say it to the Merricks too, because they'll have big decisions to make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I get to do my usual thing: watch, then move. I'd see the first robot harvesters on the big farms by year two, and I'd know if I'm the man who fixes them. I'd be all right, I think, for most of the five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the machinery dealer's evening course on farm robots once a couple of neighbours had bought them. I'd keep saving, a bit more than usual, maybe three hundred a month. By year three I'd decide: stay at Bellwood as the machine man, or go to the dealer full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like knowing the car inspection is coming and the brakes are borderline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the brakes are borderline. What's the borderline bit for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The end. Five years, then what? I'd have three good years fixing robots, then the robots get clever enough not to need me. I don't have an answer for that bit. Nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to the Merricks about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would. Ian's sensible. I'd tell him straight, if you're buying machines, let me learn them, and keep me on for the cattle till I'm good. He'd probably agree. Rob might want to sell up.

S3.say: I'd say five years is tight but doable and people should start now. I'd say the same to the Merricks, because they'll face big decisions.
S3.think: Five years lets me do my usual thing, watch then move, and I'd probably be fine for most of it. The end of it is what I can't answer.
S3.do: Takes the dealer's evening course on farm robots once a couple of neighbours have bought them. Saves about three hundred a month extra and decides by year three whether to stay at Bellwood or join the dealer full time.
S3.feel: Uneasy, like a car inspection coming with borderline brakes.
S3.quote: I'd have three good years fixing robots, then the robots get clever enough not to need me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives back his preferred rhythm of watching before moving. He's honest that he has no answer for what comes after the robots stop needing mechanics. He'd talk openly with his employer and expects them to respond differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who isn't ready by then hasn't been paying attention. I'd say it a bit softer than that in the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm fifty-three, Adam and Lina are grown, the mortgage is close to done. I'd probably get seven good years as a farm mechanic, maybe more. I'd be fine. I'd worry more for the leek gang.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Bellwood, learn the cattle properly, and do the robot course when it's been proven on a few farms. I'd keep the garage money where it is. And I'd sit down with Adam about his apprenticeship, because ten years changes what he should pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit sad for the old way, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years changes what Adam should pick. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd say be a mechanic now, earn while you can. With ten, I'd say think about where people will still want a person. Maybe the electrical side, installing things in houses. I'd want him to look around before he signs anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently with the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe put some of Dad's garage money into a pension, so at fifty-three I'm not worried. Samira would like that. She's the careful one.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty and anyone not ready by then wasn't paying attention, though I'd say it more gently in the pub.
S4.think: At fifty-three, with the kids grown and the mortgage nearly done, I'd probably get seven good years as a farm mechanic and be fine. I'd worry more for the leek gang.
S4.do: Stays at Bellwood, learns the cattle properly and takes the robot course once it's proven on a few farms. Talks with his son about which apprenticeship makes sense and considers moving some inheritance into a pension.
S4.feel: Calm, with some sadness for the old way.
S4.quote: With ten, I'd say think about where people will still want a person.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline lets his steady approach work as normal, so he's calm. The extra time mostly changes his advice to his son. He'd move some of his father's money into a pension, which he credits to his partner.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have to jump without looking, and that's not me. What would help is short courses run by the machinery dealers, paid for by the government or the farms, so people like me can switch fast. And an honest idea of which jobs last more than three years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the in-between. Everyone talks about the start and the end. But there'll be years where half the kit is robots and half is old tractors held together with wire. That's where people like me are useful. I'd want someone to plan for those years.

headlineQuote: There'll be years where half the kit is robots and half is old tractors held together with wire. That's where people like me are useful.
portrait: Victor Haddad is 43, a former car mechanic who moved to a beef and vegetable farm two and a half years ago and is still nervous around freshly calved cows. His old trade gives him a real place on the farm, and he hopes to stay useful as the person who fixes the machines, robots included. He's pragmatic, admits he sits on the fence, and likes to watch others try new things before he moves. The two-year AGI scenario forces him to jump before he's ready, while five and ten years let him keep his usual pace and turn his attention to his son's apprenticeship.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he would have to jump into something new without time to watch first.
whatWouldHelp: Short courses run by machinery dealers and paid for by government or farms, plus an honest picture of which jobs will last more than a few years.
